title: Ankara, Damascus Launch High-Level Strategic Council With Four Seas Energy Vision; Aegean-Cyprus Airspace Tensions Surge
subhead: Turkey and Syria agreed to formalize their deepening partnership through a High-Level Strategic Council, embedding Ankara in a Gulf-to-Black Sea energy and transport vision, while a spike in Aegean airspace incidents and drone activity near Cyprus added a new edge to Greek-Turkish friction.

sections.heading: Turkey-Syria Strategic Council Seals Ankara's Role in Damascus Reconstruction
sections.body:
Turkey and Syria agreed to establish a High-Level Strategic Council during a meeting in Ankara between Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan and his Syrian counterpart Asaad al-Shibani, according to Al-Monitor. The mechanism deepens political and security ties between the two governments and formalizes what is already the dominant external relationship shaping post-Assad Syria, where Turkish forces have trained and helped rebuild the Syrian army.

Shibani, who also met separately with Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin, used the visit to brief Ankara on the slow-moving integration of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) into Damascus institutions — the process most closely tied to Turkey's own bid to end the PKK's armed campaign. On Israel, he accused it of threatening regional stability and called for a return to the pre-Dec. 8, 2024 lines, while confirming that US-mediated deconfliction talks with Israel were ongoing.
sections.whyItMatters: The Strategic Council institutionalizes Turkey's influence in Syria at a moment of heightened Israeli pushback, and makes Ankara the indispensable external partner for Damascus — a position that cuts against Israel's stated goal of keeping Syria weak.

sections.heading: Four Seas Initiative: Ankara and Damascus Pitch a Hormuz Bypass
sections.body:
Fidan and Shibani also discussed activating the so-called Four Seas Initiative, an energy and transportation network Al-Monitor describes as placing Turkey and Syria at the center of a corridor from the Gulf to the Mediterranean and on to the Black Sea. The concept gains force from the ongoing Iran-US war: with the Strait of Hormuz disrupted, Le Monde reported in late July that Damascus — backed by Gulf states, Turkey and Washington — is positioning itself as an alternative energy and logistics hub connecting Gulf producers to Europe.

Syria's top diplomat struck a Gulf-friendly tone, condemning attacks on Gulf countries and calling their stability a 'fundamental pillar of regional security' — an oblique jab at Iran that aligns Ankara and Damascus with the Saudi-led bloc now bound by the Mecca Defense Pact.
sections.whyItMatters: If the Four Seas corridor matures, it would reroute Gulf energy toward Turkey and Europe via Syria, directly challenging Iran's leverage over regional shipping and giving Ankara a strategic energy asset independent of Hormuz.

sections.heading: Israel-Turkey Standoff Over Abu al-Duhur Deepens, With No Off-Ramp
sections.body:
The dispute over the Abu al-Duhur airbase escalated further on Thursday, with Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz warning Turkey against 'dangerous adventures' in Syria, while Ankara accused Israel of recklessness, Reuters reported. Israeli warplanes struck the base near Aleppo on Tuesday — hours after a Turkish delegation left — with Netanyahu's office claiming Syria was on the verge of permitting Turkish troops to deploy there, a red line Israel said it would not tolerate.

Turkey rejected the allegations as 'untenable' and aimed at legitimizing 'unlawful' strikes, arguing Netanyahu is pursuing 'expansionist and destabilizing policies' ahead of Israeli elections, per Fox News. Syrian officials say only a Turkish technical team was on site to repair a runway and control tower. Notably, US Ambassador and Syria envoy Tom Barrack publicly criticized the strike as an 'unnecessary escalation' and said he is working to establish a deconfliction mechanism among Israel, Turkey and Syria. A Middle East Eye source cited by 5Pillars suggested the strike was partly aimed at undercutting Erdogan's credibility after the Mecca Pact, telling Ankara 'they won't let him feel comfortable in Syria.'
sections.whyItMatters: Israel's willingness to bomb a base Ankara was helping rebuild, and Washington's public rebuke of its ally, signal that Turkey's Syria footprint is now a central flashpoint — with US-mediated deconfliction as the only near-term brake on direct Israel-Turkey friction.

sections.heading: Aegean and Cyprus Airspace Friction Hits a New Peak
sections.body:
Greek newspaper Kathimerini, cited by Cyprus Mail, reported that Turkish military aircraft and drones violated Greek airspace on 25 occasions on Tuesday, including eight F-16 fighter jets — two of them armed — and 17 drones, all over the Aegean. On one occasion a simulated dogfight broke out between Turkish and Greek jets; Kathimerini said it was the eighth such simulated dogfight this year.

Separately, the Cyprus air traffic controllers' union said on Thursday that flight safety around the island is 'affected by unauthorised Turkish air force aircraft and unmanned aerial vehicles' operating 'almost constantly' along critical routes and near Larnaca and Paphos airports. The union's statement follows a Turkish defense ministry announcement on July 21 of training flights south of Cyprus. These incidents sit atop the separate dispute over Turkey's planned marine parks in the eastern Mediterranean, which Le Monde reports have reignited discord between Athens and Ankara after nearly three years of relative de-escalation, alongside Greek military partnerships with Israel.
sections.whyItMatters: The uptick — armed jets, an eighth simulated dogfight this year, and sustained drone presence near Cyprus civilian airports — shows Greek-Turkish friction returning to pre-2023 levels even as Washington presses both NATO allies to stay focused on the Iran war.

sections.heading: Kurdish Peace Process: Amnesty Law Now the Leverage Point
sections.body:
The PKK amnesty framework signed by Erdogan on Aug. 19 is now being tested on the ground, as Ankara presses Damascus-aligned Kurdish structures to match it. During Shibani's Ankara visit, Turkey's priority was securing Syrian Kurdish cooperation: Al-Monitor reports Ankara wants SDF elements not integrated into the Syrian army under a Jan. 29 deal to demobilize and hand over weapons, in tandem with the PKK's commitment to dissolve and disarm.

The integration process remains contentious — Damascus resists enshrining Kurdish-language education rights in the constitution and allowing women fighters into the national army, while SDF commander Mazlum Kobane and Kurdish official Ilham Ahmed met Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa on Wednesday to discuss their roles. Shibani told reporters the sides are working to resolve 'weapons outside state control' — the exact issue that most concerns Ankara, which wants no armed structures left on its southern border.
sections.whyItMatters: The amnesty law converts Turkey's peace process from a legal framework into a negotiation lever over the SDF's fate; how Damascus integrates (or disarms) the Kurds will determine whether the PKK's dissolution pledge is reciprocated or collapses.

bottomLine: Turkey moved on three fronts on Thursday: formalizing a High-Level Strategic Council with Syria that locks Ankara into Damascus' reconstruction and a Gulf-to-Europe Four Seas energy vision, facing down Israel's warning over the Abu al-Duhur base with US-brokered deconfliction as the only safety valve, and absorbing a sharp rise in Aegean-Cyprus airspace incidents that signals Greek-Turkish tension is climbing again. The strategic thread is Ankara's bid to consolidate itself as the indispensable power in its Levantine and eastern Mediterranean neighborhood — and the pushback it is drawing from Israel, and increasingly from Athens and Nicosia, in response.
sources: Al-Monitor, Reuters, Fox News, Cyprus Mail (citing Kathimerini), Le Monde, 5Pillars (citing Middle East Eye), AP News, Greek Reporter
